title: The dead
hook: you can forgive someone who has died

segments.voice: Yesterday, forgiving parents. Your line was they were young too. Did the small sting soften at all? Today, the people who can no longer hear an apology, or offer one. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

A phone still holds a voicemail from someone who has died. It's two years old. It's about nothing, a question about dinner. And underneath it sits an argument that was never settled, because there was supposed to be time. Now there isn't. The person who could apologize is gone, and so is the person who could hear one. It's easy to assume that means the door has closed. Some very old texts say otherwise. Today: the dead.
screen: `A VOICEMAIL ABOUT NOTHING.` → `AN ARGUMENT NEVER SETTLED.` → `IS THE DOOR CLOSED?`

segments.voice: First, a king who gets the news. In the second book of Samuel, King David's son Absalom has turned against him, raised an army, and driven his father out of Jerusalem. In the battle that follows, Absalom is killed. When the messenger arrives, David doesn't celebrate a victory. He goes up to a room over the gate and weeps: "O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! would God I had died for thee." A son who tried to take his father's throne, and the father's cry is his name, over and over. Whatever lay between them, David's love goes on speaking to his son after he is gone. Second, the other direction. The Talmud records a teaching for someone who wronged a person who has since died. They can't go and appease the person anymore, so the teaching says to bring others with them to the grave and say there, aloud, that they wronged this person. The relationship still carries weight after death. The words are still worth saying, in a place, with witnesses. Third, forgiving the dead. If an apology can be offered to the dead, forgiveness can be offered to them too. The other person doesn't need to take part. They never did. Forgiveness, as this whole block has been saying, happens in the one who forgives. Saying it out loud gives it a time and a place, so it isn't only a thought that comes and goes. Fourth, what it doesn't require. It doesn't require pretending they were someone else. David's son still rebelled. The wrong still happened. Forgiving the dead is releasing what you're still holding, not rewriting who they were. It still counts.
screen: `O MY SON ABSALOM.` · `WORDS SPOKEN AT THE GRAVE.` · `THEY DON'T NEED TO TAKE PART.` · `RELEASE, NOT REWRITE.` · then, large: `IT STILL COUNTS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who has died, with whom something was left unsettled. If that's too heavy today, choose something small, or simply sit with their memory. Picture them, as clearly as you can. Then, if you're somewhere you can, say aloud, quietly, what you forgive them for. One sentence is enough. If you're not alone, move your lips without sound. Then sit with whatever comes. If you pray, you can name them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The dead. Forgiveness, or an apology, offered to someone who has died, spoken in a time and place, even though they can't answer. Today's word.
Your line: it still counts. Today, if the unsettled thing comes back, remember you said it aloud, and that it still counts. Day nine hundred eighty-three.

howItsDone: The Talmud describes going to the grave of someone you wronged and saying aloud, before others, that you wronged them; some people visit graves to speak to those they've lost, sometimes to settle what was left unsaid.

fork.setup: you're King David. your son Absalom raised an army against you and drove you from Jerusalem. a messenger arrives: Absalom is dead. what do you do?
options: thank the messenger for the victory.
go up to the room over the gate and weep for him.
say nothing and return to the city.
fork.reveal: David weeps and cries his son's name over and over: "would God I had died for thee."

trapdoor: what you thought: once someone dies, it's too late to forgive or be forgiven.
what it means: forgiveness and apology can still be spoken, in a time and place, without a reply.
what a scholar hears: the Talmud gives a procedure for asking forgiveness of the dead, at the grave, with others present.

notes: Yoma 87a: one who wronged a person who has died brings people (the Talmud says ten) to the grave and says 'I have sinned against the Lord God of Israel and against this one'. The number is left out of the voice per the claims rule. Confirm the paraphrase.
2 Samuel 15–18 summary (Absalom's revolt, David fleeing Jerusalem, Absalom killed in battle) is paraphrased; confirm.
Hook voicemail 'two years old' is a fictional scene detail, not a claim.
howItsDone: 'some people visit graves to speak to those they've lost' (softened from 'in many places').

Editor pass: the teach said David's 'first words' on hearing the news were Absalom's name, but 2 Samuel 18:29 and 18:32 have him first ask whether the young man Absalom is safe; changed to 'the father's cry is his name'. howItsDone 'in many places' softened to 'some people'.
Audit pass: 'David's love speaks to him after he is gone' was ambiguous (whose love, to whom); clarified.
